leading_positions.synthesis: Three members prefer a two-name Katori and Ye prize for optical lattice clocks, and all three give the same two laureates. They share the case that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle for neutral atoms, that accuracy near 1e-18 has been reproduced and cross-compared by several independent laboratories, and that the credit is clean. They also share the main weakness: the fundamental-physics output so far is limits, the redefinition of the second has not happened, and the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes invite an incrementalism objection. They differ on emphasis (Kroll and Lindroth stress the lattice concept, Lindroth proposes centring the citation on millimetre-scale relativistic redshift) and on whether a third name is needed (Kroll leaves it open, Lindroth would hold at two). Four other members who do not prefer it rank it lower or call it a tool: Danielsson, Johansson and Mehlig state this explicitly, and Olsson would rank it above B038 or B022. Pearce is the chair and a supporter, so this summary should be read with that disclosed.

Three members prefer a topological insulator prize, and their shared ground is the Kane-Mele prediction, the HgTe edge-transport measurement, and about two decades of independent confirmation across platforms. They do not share the same trio. Danielsson and Olsson propose Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, which keeps the 3D ARPES discovery. Mehlig now proposes Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, having moved Mele in place of Hasan in round 1, and argues that Mele is inseparable from Kane and that 3D credit is diffuse. Olsson makes her support conditional on a check of what Mele contributed in the 2005 papers. All three accept that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the credit and that the 2016 topological-phases prize needs an explicit distinction. Eriksson, Kroll and Pearce name B006 as an alternative; Johansson would not oppose it if the allocation can be settled.

Eriksson alone prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer, as a quantitative 2011 prediction confirmed in 2018 and reproduced by many groups. Danielsson, Mehlig and Olsson list it as an alternative. Olsson and Mehlig regard it as a candidate for a later cycle because the pairing mechanism is unsettled and the field is about eight years old; Johansson raises device disorder as well. Eriksson himself flags the open attribution questions (Dean, Cao, earlier flat-band theory) and his own DFT background.

Johansson alone prefers circuit QED with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf, framed around the strong-coupling regime and dispersive readout rather than quantum computing. Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig name it as an alternative. Objections from several members concern proximity to the 2025 circuit prize and the omission of Girvin and Huang. Johansson argues the discoveries are distinct and has disclosed a possible conflict and invited discounting.

areas_of_agreement: All eight members name their own preferred configuration as a single prize part with three names or fewer, and no member proposes a multi-part prize as preferred, although Mehlig raises a two-part prize with B047 or B017 as a possible alternative.

Optical lattice clocks (B047) and topological insulators (B006) are each described by members on both sides as strong on scientific merit and independent confirmation; the disagreement is about novelty and attribution rather than whether the results are real.

Members who do not prefer a candidate consistently accept that its results are reproduced; the reservations are about overlap with earlier prizes (2005, 2012, 2016, 2025), maturity, and who is missing from the credit.

Several members, including Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce, state that the other candidate they rank high would be an acceptable or serious second choice, and B006 is named as an alternative by Eriksson, Kroll and Pearce.

Girvin and Huang are acknowledged as missing from circuit QED by Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are acknowledged as missing from B006 by Danielsson, Johansson, Kroll, Mehlig and Olsson.
scientific_disputes: Whether optical lattice clocks (B047) are a distinct discovery (the magic-wavelength principle, many-atom control, millimetre-scale redshift) or an excellent refinement of the toolbox honoured in 2005 and 2012. Danielsson, Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson raise this; Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce answer that the lattice concept is a new principle.

Whether null results and limits on constants and ultralight dark matter count as a discovery. Danielsson calls the clocks an instrument rather than a discovery pending the redefinition of the second or a signal; Kroll replies that limits and geodesy measurements are information about nature.

Whether circuit QED (B038) is a different phenomenon from the 2025 macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, as Johansson and Mehlig argue, or a natural sequel that argues for waiting, as Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce suggest.

Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize leaves room for the Z2 topological insulator. Danielsson, Mehlig and Olsson say it is distinct (time-reversal-invariant topology in real materials); Johansson and Pearce regard the novelty question as unresolved.

Whether the IceCube diffuse flux alone (B048) is a settled discovery separate from the few source identifications; Pearce, Johansson and Lindroth discuss this, and Lindroth notes that KM3NeT has not yet confirmed it independently.
attribution_disputes: B006: whether the third name is Hasan (Danielsson, Olsson; Pearce proposed this in the shortlist data) or Mele (Mehlig, and Johansson and Lindroth in their proposals). Choosing Mele leaves the 3D ARPES discovery unrecognised, and choosing Hasan separates Mele from Kane. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Fu, Moore and others for 3D, fall outside any three-name cut, and Zhang is deceased.

B047: Katori and Ye are the pair every proposal names, but Kroll and Lindroth note that other lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, Yb groups) could have a claim and disagree on whether a third name is warranted.

B038: Girvin and Huang co-authored the 2004 proposal and are not in the credited trio, and Eriksson and Pearce note that the Yale and Devoret links complicate the narrative; Johansson accepts the gap.

B017: whether three names (Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald, Bistritzer) is a defensible cut given the roles of Cao, Dean and earlier flat-band theory, and Olsson's concern that the group leader is credited while the measurements were made by junior authors.
B048: whether two names (Halzen and Karle) can represent a large collaboration given AMANDA and DUMAND; Pearce and Kroll treat this as a serious obstacle.
maturity_disputes: B006 is called the most mature case by Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce because of about twenty years of independent confirmation across platforms.

B017 is called young (about eight years) by Mehlig, Olsson and Johansson, with the pairing mechanism and device disorder unresolved. Eriksson argues that the prediction-confirmation step has already succeeded and that open mechanisms do not undermine the discovery.
B047: Eriksson and Olsson ask whether the redefinition of the second should come first, while Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce argue the clock result is already settled by independent comparisons.
B048 and B038: Pearce, Kroll and Lindroth state that IceCube source identification needs further maturing; Eriksson suggests that circuit QED may be better after a few years given the 2025 prize.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson (B038 first): theorist in superconducting circuits at Chalmers and director of WACQT, which depends on the circuit QED architecture; he knows Wallraff and Schoelkopf as peers and offers that the committee consider recusal or discounting.

Kroll (B047 first): spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during his PhD, and Jun Ye is associated with Hall's JILA group (a distant lineage, not a collaboration); is also in WACQT leadership, overlapping institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers base on B038, and is on the management team of a Lund spin-off in an unrelated field.

Olsson: Fellow at the University of Tokyo (Katori, B047) since 2025 and lectured at Tohoku University (Miyazaki, B015) in 2026; she describes these as institutional contacts, and records that Johansson is a Chalmers colleague.
Pearce (chair, B047 first): no conflict for B047, B006 or B048, but he is a detector builder in astroparticle physics and discloses closeness to IceCube (B048), which he lists as an alternative.
Lindroth: collaborates with a 2023 laureate (L'Huillier) and with Lund and ETH groups, which she says bears on other candidates and not on B047, B038 or B048.

Mehlig: in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson, with no known collaboration. Danielsson and Eriksson report no specific conflict; Eriksson notes his expertise overlap with B017 and B006 as expertise only.
questions_for_round2: For B006, if the committee were to adopt it, who holds the third seat: Hasan, who anchors the 3D discovery, or Mele, who co-wrote the 2005 papers with Kane? What did each 2005 paper contribute, as Olsson asks, and can a citation be worded to the quantum spin Hall effect and HgTe observation so as to answer the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit?

For B047, does the lattice-clock concept stand distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, as the proponents say and as Danielsson, Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson doubt? Is the redefinition of the second a precondition, or can the lattice scheme and its accuracy carry a citation on its own?
For B047, is Katori and Ye the final credit, or does a third name from SYRTE or the Yb groups belong, and can that be settled without a priority dispute?

For B038, can the committee state what separates strong light-matter coupling in circuits from the 2025 prize, and is the Girvin and Huang omission acceptable? Given Johansson's disclosure, how should his support for B038 be weighed?
For B017, is the correlated-insulator and superconductivity result settled by enough independent groups to count as mature now, as Eriksson asks to be shown, or is it a candidate for a later year?

Is the committee prepared to choose between the broadest ballot support (B006, with an unresolved third name) and the cleanest credit (B047, with narrower support), and what would change any member's order between them?
Is there a natural two-part prize pairing (for example B006 or B017 with B047, as Mehlig raised), or should round 2 keep to single-part configurations?
What is the status of B048 and B015 for round 2, given that no member now prefers them, and should any member who named them as an alternative restate why?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 splits the committee into two three-member blocs, optical lattice clocks (Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce) and topological insulators (Danielsson, Mehlig, Olsson), plus single-member preferences for twisted bilayer graphene (Eriksson) and circuit QED (Johansson). The bloc preferring B006 is not unanimous on the laureates, since Mehlig's trio differs from the other two, while the three who prefer B047 agree on the same two names. The members who changed their preferred position (Olsson from B015 to B006, Pearce from B048 to B047, and Mehlig on the third laureate) did so after reading the opening ballots. The main points for round 2 are the allocation of the third seat in B006, the novelty of B047 relative to earlier prizes, and the overlap and credit questions around B038, and the committee should note that the chair supports one of the two leading positions.
